name: Forskolin

card.summary: A Coleus plant compound that raises cAMP in cells and is sold as a fat burner; supplement claims rest on small, low-quality studies.
card.aka: Coleonol, Coleus forskohlii extract, Indian coleus, makandi
card.note: A standard lab tool for raising cAMP; Wikipedia describes the early weight-loss studies as low quality and inconclusive.

quick.overview:
Forskolin is a diterpene isolated from the roots of Coleus forskohlii (also called Coleus barbatus or Plectranthus barbatus), a plant used in Ayurvedic medicine. In laboratories it is a standard reagent for switching on the cell-signalling molecule cAMP.

Supplement makers market Coleus extract for fat loss and lean mass. Wikipedia describes the early human weight-loss studies as low quality with inconclusive results.
quick.mechanism: Forskolin directly activates adenylyl cyclase, the enzyme that makes cyclic AMP (cAMP). cAMP is a second messenger that acts through protein kinase A and EPAC. In fat cells, raised cAMP is associated with fat breakdown (lipolysis), which is the basis for the weight-loss claims.
quick.risks: Wikipedia gives only chemical hazard information and does not describe adverse effects in people. Because forskolin influences cAMP signalling in many tissues, including heart and blood vessels, laboratory work has studied cardiovascular effects. Human safety data for long-term supplement use are limited.

lead: Forskolin, also called coleonol, is a labdane diterpene obtained from the roots of Coleus forskohlii, a plant in the mint family used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine. [1][2] It was identified in the 1970s and became a widely used biochemical tool because it activates adenylyl cyclase and raises intracellular cAMP. [1][3]

Dietary supplements containing Coleus extract are marketed for fat loss and body composition. Wikipedia characterises the early weight-loss research as low quality and inconclusive, and notes that newer laboratory work suggests bioavailability strongly affects any anti-obesity effect. [1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that some clinical studies reported modest fat-mass reductions. [2]
Other human research has focused on glaucoma and, in smaller studies, on supplementation with exercise. [4][5][6]

paras: According to Grokipedia, forskolin was first isolated in 1974 at the Central Drug Research Institute in Lucknow, India, from Coleus forskohlii roots during a screen for blood-pressure-lowering plants, and was initially named coleonol. [2] Hoechst India researchers later worked out its structure and renamed it forskolin, after the botanist Peter Forsskal. [2]

A 1981 paper in PNAS described forskolin as a unique diterpene activator of adenylate cyclase in membranes and in intact cells, and the compound became a standard way to raise cAMP in cell experiments. [3] Papers on CREB phosphorylation and cAMP-responsive genes frequently use forskolin as the stimulus. [7]

Forskolin activates adenylyl cyclase directly, which raises cAMP; downstream effects include activation of protein kinase A and the exchange factor EPAC. [1][3] Derivatives such as colforsin daropate have been studied for heart failure and bronchoconstriction. [1]

Supplements are sold on the premise that cAMP elevation promotes fat burning and supports lean mass. Wikipedia notes that early weight-loss studies were of low quality and that conclusions cannot be drawn. [1]

Research interest has included glaucoma, asthma, heart failure and hypertension, though forskolin is not an approved treatment for these. [2] Two registered glaucoma studies of forskolin on intraocular pressure were withdrawn. [4][8]

Registered human studies include a glaucoma retinal-nerve-fibre study (NCT01254006), two withdrawn glaucoma pressure trials (NCT00864578, NCT00863811), and trials of multi-ingredient supplements with exercise, such as the TRIM MUSCLE study of 51 overweight or obese adults (NCT05384431). [4][8][9][6] Results from these registrations are not described in the available sources, and forskolin is combined with other ingredients in several. Wikipedia's overall assessment is that earlier weight-loss studies were low quality and inconclusive. [1]
Wikipedia lists a safety data sheet classification of acute dermal toxicity category 4 for the pure chemical, and does not describe adverse effects in people. [1]

timeline.event: Forskolin (coleonol) is isolated from Coleus forskohlii at the Central Drug Research Institute, India (per Grokipedia). [2]
Hoechst India researchers work out the structure and rename it forskolin (per Grokipedia). [2]
PNAS paper describes forskolin as an activator of adenylate cyclase in membranes and intact cells. [3]
All nine biosynthetic genes for forskolin are expressed in yeast. [1]
Total chemical synthesis of racemic forskolin reported. [1]
